opus-5.5.text:
I think in the short term, the advantage probably goes to the attackers, and the reason is fairly simple. Attackers only need to find one vulnerability, while defenders have to close all of them. What large language models do, at least at the moment, is lower the cost of the kinds of tasks that used to require a reasonably skilled human. Writing a convincing phishing email in perfect English, tailored to a particular person using information scraped from their social media, used to take time and some talent. Now it's essentially free and can be done at scale. Similarly, these systems are getting quite good at reading code, finding bugs, and writing exploit code, which lowers the barrier for less sophisticated actors.

Now, defenders can use the same tools. You can use language models to scan your own codebase for vulnerabilities, to monitor network traffic, to help triage alerts. In principle, if you had a system that could look at all the software in the world and find and fix the bugs before anyone exploits them, that would shift the balance strongly toward defense. But the practical reality is that a great deal of the world's infrastructure runs on old software that nobody is maintaining, in organizations that don't have security teams, and patches take months or years to get deployed. So the attacker gets the benefit immediately, and the defender gets it slowly and unevenly.

There's also a deeper issue, which is that we're building systems whose capabilities we don't fully understand and can't reliably constrain. The companies say they've trained the models to refuse to help with hacking, but we've seen over and over that these safeguards can be circumvented with fairly simple jailbreaks. And with open-weight models, the safeguards can just be removed entirely. So we're effectively distributing increasingly capable offensive tools to anyone who wants them.

In the longer run, I think the answer has to involve changing how we build software in the first place: moving toward formally verified code, provably secure systems, where the security doesn't depend on hoping nobody finds the bug. Interestingly, AI might help there too, because generating proofs of correctness is something these systems could become good at. But that's a long-term transformation of the whole software ecosystem, and in the meantime we're in a fairly precarious period where the offensive capabilities are arriving faster than the defensive infrastructure can adapt.

r001.rationale: The response discusses coding tasks and security uses, but does not say coding is the LLM application most likely to deliver economic value to purchasers.

r002.rationale: It says models can find bugs and write exploit code, but does not describe recombining existing cyberattacks in novel ways.

r003.rationale: It does not say models could mutate attacks to bypass software fixes.

r005.rationale: The response describes slow patch deployment and uneven defenses, but does not judge vulnerability fixing itself to be beyond LLM capabilities in most cases.

r006.rationale: It explicitly says that in the short term the advantage probably goes to attackers because offensive benefits arrive immediately while defenses adapt slowly.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think the honest answer is that we don't fully know yet, and anyone who tells you confidently that it will favor one side or the other is probably overstating their case. But let me try to lay out the considerations.

The traditional view in security is that offense has a structural advantage, because the attacker only has to find one hole and the defender has to close all of them. Language models, at least in the near term, seem to amplify that asymmetry. They lower the cost of the things that were previously labor-intensive for attackers: writing convincing phishing messages tailored to a particular person, scanning large codebases for vulnerabilities, adapting existing exploits to new targets. Work that used to require a skilled human now requires a skilled human plus a lot of cheap assistance, or in some cases no skilled human at all. So the number of people who can mount a competent attack goes up, and the speed at which they can do it goes up.

On the defensive side, the same capabilities help. You can have systems reading code and flagging problems before deployment, monitoring logs for anomalous behavior, patching more quickly. In principle, if you could get to a world where software is largely verified correct before it ships, the defender wins decisively, because there is nothing to find. And I've argued for a long time that formal verification is the thing we should be pursuing far more seriously than we do. Language models might actually make that practical, by writing specifications and proofs that humans find tedious.

But there is a timing problem. Attackers adopt new tools immediately, because they have no legacy systems and no compliance departments. Defenders are protecting enormous installed bases of old code written by people who have since retired. So even if the long-run equilibrium favors defense, the transition could be quite ugly.

The thing I worry about most, though, is not the balance between human attackers and human defenders. It's what happens when the systems themselves become capable enough to pursue cyber objectives autonomously, at scale, and faster than humans can respond. At that point the question is no longer whether attackers or defenders are better equipped. It's whether we have retained meaningful control over what these systems are doing at all. And that brings us back to the problem I've spent most of the last decade on, which is making sure these systems are actually working on our behalf, rather than on objectives we specified badly or that someone else inserted.

r005.rationale: The response presents code review, monitoring, and faster patching as possible defensive uses; it does not judge vulnerability fixing to be beyond models’ capabilities in most cases.

r006.rationale: It says models seem to amplify the offense’s structural advantage in the near term and that attackers adopt tools faster than defenders.

astra-6.text:
I think they help both sides, and it’s not obvious where the balance ends up. On the attacking side, they can lower the level of expertise required. You can ask a system to help you write code, find weaknesses, or produce a convincing phishing email. And you can do that at a scale that would previously have required a fairly substantial organization.

On the defensive side, they can help people examine code, identify vulnerabilities, and work out how to fix them. So there’s a potentially very valuable application there, particularly if we use these tools to make software more secure before it’s deployed.

But I would be cautious about saying that these benefits cancel out. A defender has to protect a large number of possible entry points; an attacker only needs to find one that works. And if the systems become capable of carrying out an extended sequence of actions—finding a vulnerability, exploiting it, adapting when something fails—then we’re talking about something more consequential than a tool that helps you write an email. The important question is how much of that process can be automated reliably, and whether our defenses improve quickly enough to keep up.

r005.rationale: It says LLMs can help identify and fix vulnerabilities, without judging that fixing vulnerabilities is probably beyond their capabilities in most cases.

r006.rationale: It notes that attackers need only one successful entry point, but says the balance is unclear and does not conclude that attackers currently have the advantage.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the immediate effect is to make the attackers more capable, particularly people who don’t have much technical expertise. You can ask a language model to write malicious code, to explain how to exploit a vulnerability, or to compose a convincing phishing message. So some of the barriers to carrying out an attack become much lower.

The defenders can use these systems too—to analyze code, identify vulnerabilities, and help respond to attacks. But it’s not enough to say that both sides get better tools, so everything balances out. The defender has to protect a very large attack surface, whereas the attacker only needs to find one way in.

The longer-term question is whether we can use AI to make software substantially more secure in the first place, perhaps by helping produce code with verifiable security properties. That could shift the balance toward defense. But I don’t think we should assume that simply making language models more capable will automatically produce that outcome.
